1: Welcome the group. Frame the session in one line: client control is what separates a recruiter who takes orders from one who runs the process. Today is about three things: selling a candidate in with conviction, building a pitch that answers objections before they come up, and keeping control of the timeline from brief to close. It’s practical, the second half is role-play, so ask everyone to have a live candidate and a live job in mind.
2: Run through the three outcomes. Check everyone has the pre-work: a live job and a candidate they’d like to submit. If anyone doesn’t, pair them with someone who does for the role-play.
3: Ask the room to self-score: for each row, which column did you sit in on your last placement or lost deal? Don’t make it a confession; make it a baseline. The point is that control is built at every stage, not grabbed at the end. Spend about 5 minutes here.
4: Selling in a candidate is building a compelling, evidence-based case, not forwarding a CV. Walk through the four parts left to right. Then read the example aloud and ask the room to spot each part: outcome (takes the migration off your plate), context (same move, similar company), proof (cost reduction, use a real figure from your candidate), logistics (package, notice, other process, decision date). The bracketed figures are placeholders: trainees should drop in their own candidate’s real numbers. Point out that the ask for a decision date is part of the pitch, not an afterthought.
5: Conviction is earned in the prep, not performed on the call. Ask: who has submitted a candidate this month they weren’t sure about? What happened? Usually the client picked up on the hesitation. Stress pre-empting concerns: if you raise the short tenure first with a clear explanation, it becomes context. If the client finds it, it becomes a red flag. Finish on the tip, it’s the quality bar for every submission.
6: The four-step structure keeps a pitch under two minutes. Logistics go last but must never be skipped: a great pitch that hides a salary gap or a 90-day notice period destroys trust later. Remind the group that an objection you can’t answer confidently usually means you didn’t prepare enough before the call. Have each person write their top three objections for their own live job now (3 minutes); they’ll use them in the role-play.
7: Run this as call-and-response: read the objection, let a trainee answer before you reveal the reframe. The pattern in every reframe: acknowledge it, ask a clarifying question, answer with evidence, then close for the next step. “Let’s see a few more” is often a sign the client isn’t sure what good looks like; that is a requalification moment, not a sourcing one. Never use a candidate’s other processes as leverage unless they are real.
8: Go back to the whiteboard tally from the opening (who had a client go quiet this month). Ask those people to check the red list: how many signs apply to their job right now? Two or more means control has slipped and they should use the reset on the next slide this week. The green list is preventive; most lost control starts at the brief, when no timeline was agreed.
9: This is the practical version of the “set the timeline upfront” point on the last slide. The dates in the table are an example, not a rule; adjust them to the market and the seniority of the role. What matters is that every stage has a date and a feedback deadline, and that the client has confirmed it in writing. Ask: how many of your live jobs have a written timeline today? Action for everyone: send one this week on your highest-priority job. When a client misses a date, you now have something to point back to, without it becoming personal.
10: The reset works because it is honest, specific and ends with a concrete ask. If the client can’t commit to new dates, regrade the job (see the Job Specification module): a role with no committed timeline is a C job, and your time should move to A jobs. Have each trainee write their own version of the script for one live job before moving on.
11: Groups of three: seller, client, observer. The client should be realistic, not hostile; the goal is practice, not a gotcha. Observers score each element of the sell-in framework from 1 to 5 and give one thing to keep and one thing to change. Timekeep strictly. In the room debrief, ask: which objection was hardest to answer, and what would have prepared you for it? Capture the best reframes on the whiteboard and share them in the team channel afterwards.
12: Give everyone 3 minutes to write their three takeaways. Managers: review the four actions in next week’s one-to-ones. Ask to see the written timeline and the reset call outcome. Suggested follow-up: a 15-minute desk role-play with the manager on one live submission.
13: Open the floor for questions. Close by connecting client control to the next module: once you control the process, interview prep and pre-closing are where you convert it into an offer that lands.
